titre: Sudbury, 1.85 Billion Years Ago: A Comet May Have Ended Banded Iron
accroche: 1.85 billion years ago, banded iron deposition stops cold. A USGS study sees the mark of a giant impact, not a slow ocean evolution.
contenu_vulgarise:
Across northern Canada and the United States, rocks striped with red and gray bands stretch for hundreds of kilometers: these are banded iron formations, the ore that fed the steel industry of the twentieth century, from Minnesota to Lake Superior. Their bands tell, layer by layer, a precise episode in the ocean's history.

## Iron the water used to dissolve, and then stopped dissolving

Before the atmosphere held oxygen in lasting quantity, the deep oceans were rich in dissolved ferrous iron (Fe²⁺), carried in by the weathering of continents and by hydrothermal vents. As soon as this iron rose toward surface water where photosynthesis was producing oxygen, it oxidized into insoluble ferric iron (Fe³⁺) and settled to the bottom in layers alternating with silica. This is the model geologist Preston Cloud proposed as early as 1968: cyanobacteria, shielded by the very iron that absorbed the oxygen they produced, would have kept this cycle running for more than a billion years. The oldest known formations, in Greenland, date to 3.7–3.8 billion years ago; the most massive, in Western Australia, were deposited between 2,470 and 2,450 million years ago, over more than 900 meters of thickness.

## An abrupt end, not a slow extinction

Around 1.85 billion years ago, banded iron deposition stops almost everywhere, within a few million years. The explanation that first comes to mind is a gradual oxygenation of the deep ocean, which would eventually have stopped ferrous iron from accumulating. But in 2009, two USGS researchers, John Slack and William Cannon, propose another cause for this precise cutoff: it coincides with the impact of the giant Sudbury bolide, in present-day Ontario, also dated to 1.85 billion years ago. According to their study published in the journal Geology, this impact would have mixed the oxygenated surface waters and the anoxic deep waters all at once, bringing the whole ocean to a slightly oxygenated state, enough to permanently block the transport of hydrothermal iron toward the continental margins where banded iron was forming.

## What this shifts

The usual story of Earth's oxygenation is one of a slope: life produces oxygen, the atmosphere and ocean gradually load up with it. The Sudbury hypothesis introduces an extraterrestrial jolt into this otherwise biological narrative: a crater with an original diameter of about 130 kilometers, among the largest ever identified on Earth, dated to within a million years by isotopic dating of zircons, may have compressed into one geological instant what photosynthesis took hundreds of millions of years to do. Banded iron does not only tell the story of oxygen's rise, then: it also lets scientists date, to within a million years, the day a rock from space may have stirred an entire ocean.

carte.punch: A rock that fell from space may have stopped a billion years of banded iron.
carte.idee: The deposition of banded iron, evidence of oxygen's arrival in ancient oceans, stops abruptly 1.85 billion years ago. A 2009 USGS study links this cutoff to the impact of the giant Sudbury bolide, dated to the same period, which may have mixed the ocean's waters all at once.

quiz.question: Why did the end of banded iron deposition around 1.85 billion years ago surprise geologists, according to Slack and Cannon's 2009 study?
choix: Because it shows that oxygen never appeared in ancient oceans, even after the Great Oxidation Event
Because it is too fast for simple gradual oxygenation, and coincides with a giant impact dated to the same period
Because no banded iron formation had ever been found on Earth before that exact date
Because banded iron, according to this study, actually contains no trace of iron oxidation
quiz.explication: Slack and Cannon, researchers at the USGS, link the abrupt end of deposition to the impact of the Sudbury bolide, dated to the same 1.85 billion years, which would have mixed the ocean's waters all at once. The other claims contradict either the chronology (banded iron exists as early as 3.7–3.8 Ga) or the chemical oxidation mechanism these rocks are built on.
